passages.text: And in response I said, “Then those who do wrong are not responsible, since it is by God’s judgment that they wrong the righteous.” Peter said, “They most certainly do sin, for they have given themselves over to sinning. Therefore, with this knowledge, he chooses some from among them to punish justly those who have come to regret their former sins, so that, for the righteous, through punishment of this kind, the evil deeds done before their reorientation may be forgiven, while the ungodly punishers, who desire to maltreat others and are unwilling to reorient, have been permitted to maltreat the righteous in order to fill up the measure of their own penalty. For without God’s counsel not even a sparrow can fall into a trap; in the same way, even the hairs of the righteous are numbered by God.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅθεν εἰδὼς ἀπ᾽ αὐτῶν ἐκλέγεται τιμωρεῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Therefore, with this knowledge, he chooses some from among them to punish
lexical_decisions.rationale: The subject is understood contextually as God, while the people chosen from among the wrongdoers are the understood subjects of the infinitive “to punish.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοὺς ἐπὶ τοῖς προτέροις ἁμαρτήμασιν μεταμεληθέντας δικαίως
lexical_decisions.chosen: those who have come to regret their former sins ... justly
lexical_decisions.rationale: μεταμέλομαι is distinguished from the subsequent μετάνοια language and rendered as regret. δικαίως is attached to the justice of the punishment; it could instead describe their regretting as rightly done.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸ τῆς μετανοίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: before their reorientation
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering follows the supplied terminology policy for μετάνοια while not adding an unstated destination such as “toward God.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μετανοεῖν μὴ θέλουσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: are unwilling to reorient
lexical_decisions.rationale: The moral redirection sense of μετανοεῖν is retained without an invented intensifier or destination.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς ἀναπλήρωσιν ἰδίας κολάσεως
lexical_decisions.chosen: in order to fill up the measure of their own penalty
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀναπλήρωσις denotes filling up or completing, while κόλασις here is the punishment accruing to the ungodly agents.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἄνευ γὰρ τῆς τοῦ θεοῦ βουλῆς οὐδὲ στρουθὸς ἐν παγίδι ἐνπεσεῖν ἔχει
lexical_decisions.chosen: without God’s counsel not even a sparrow can fall into a trap
lexical_decisions.rationale: βουλή is “counsel” or “purpose,” and the ἔχει plus infinitive construction is represented idiomatically by “can.” The explicitly named trap is retained.

passages.text: The righteous person is the one who, for the sake of what reason approves, fights against nature. For example, everyone has it by nature to love those who love them, but the righteous person tries also to love enemies, to bless those who revile him, and, moreover, to pray for enemies. He has mercy on those who wrong him; therefore he also refrains from wronging them in return. Likewise, he blesses those who curse him, gives way to those who strike him, withdraws before those who pursue him, greets those who do not greet him, shares what he has with those who have nothing, wins over the angry person, reconciles the enemy, exhorts the disobedient person, instructs the unbeliever, comforts the mourner, endures when abused, and does not become indignant when treated ungratefully. Having committed himself to loving his neighbor as himself, he has not feared poverty; rather, by distributing his own possessions to those who have nothing, he becomes poor. Nor, indeed, does he punish someone who sins. For the one who loves his neighbor as himself knows that, if he himself had sinned, he would not want to be punished; in the same way, he does not punish those who sin. And just as he wants to be flattered, blessed, and honored, and to have all his sins forgiven him, he himself does this same thing for his neighbor, because he loves that person as himself. In a word, what he wants for himself he also wants for his neighbor. For this is the law of God and of the prophets; this is the teaching of the truth. All this, then, is perfect love toward every human being and is the male part of humaneness, while showing mercy is its female part. This consists in feeding the hungry, providing drink to the thirsty, clothing the naked, visiting the sick, receiving a stranger, helping the person in prison to the extent possible while being sprinkled upon, and, in short, having mercy on anyone amid misfortunes.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ τοῦ εὐλόγου ἕνεκα τῇ φύσει μαχόμενος
lexical_decisions.chosen: the one who, for the sake of what reason approves, fights against nature
lexical_decisions.rationale: τὸ εὔλογον denotes what is reasonable or warranted by reason. The author’s image of conflict with nature is retained.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: φιλοῦντας φιλεῖν ... ἐχθροὺς ἀγαπᾶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: to love those who love them ... to love enemies
lexical_decisions.rationale: The first expression uses φιλέω reciprocally and the second uses ἀγαπάω. English “love” is used for both, while the distinct Greek roots and the contrast between natural reciprocity and enemy-love are disclosed here.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: προσαδικεῖσθαι ἀπέχεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: refrains from wronging them in return
lexical_decisions.rationale: The middle infinitive is understood contextually as retaliatory wrongdoing. A more formally passive reading, “refrains from being wronged further,” is grammatically possible but fits the surrounding acts of nonretaliation less readily.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τύπτουσιν συγχωρεῖ
lexical_decisions.chosen: gives way to those who strike him
lexical_decisions.rationale: συγχωρεῖ can mean either “gives way” or, in later usage, “forgives.” “Gives way” preserves the movement imagery reinforced by the following ὑποχωρεῖ, while “forgives those who strike him” remains a viable alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς αὐτὸς ἁμαρτήσας οἶδεν τιμωρηθῆναι μὴ θέλειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: knows that, if he himself had sinned, he would not want to be punished
lexical_decisions.rationale: The aorist participle is read conditionally. It could instead refer to his actual past sin: “knows that, having himself sinned, he does not want to be punished.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κολακεύεσθαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: to be flattered
lexical_decisions.rationale: The potentially uncomfortable force of κολακεύω is preserved rather than softened to “treated kindly.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ ἄρρεν μέρος ... τὸ θῆλυ μέρος
lexical_decisions.chosen: the male part ... its female part
lexical_decisions.rationale: The author’s gendered division of perfect love and mercy is preserved without harmonization or explanation in the translation text.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: φιλανθρωπίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: humaneness
lexical_decisions.rationale: φιλανθρωπία denotes benevolence or love toward humanity; “humaneness” is used consistently here and in the following passage.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ ἐν εἱρκτῇ κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν ἐπιραινόμενον βοηθεῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: helping the person in prison to the extent possible while being sprinkled upon
lexical_decisions.rationale: The accusative participle ἐπιραινόμενον is taken as agreeing with the understood accusative subject of βοηθεῖν—the helper—rather than with the dative prisoner. Its passive force is represented literally by “while being sprinkled upon.” A formally possible middle interpretation is “while sprinkling oneself upon,” but the contextual significance of either image remains uncertain.

source_issues.source_quote: τῷ ἐν εἱρκτῇ κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν ἐπιραινόμενον βοηθεῖν
source_issues.issue: The image-checked printed form ἐπιραινόμενον is an accusative singular middle/passive participle. It can belong to the understood accusative subject of βοηθεῖν, namely the person helping the prisoner, so the supplied wording admits the literal passive representation “while being sprinkled upon” without emendation. The middle alternative “while sprinkling oneself upon” is also formally possible. What the sprinkling signifies in this context remains uncertain, and no object or further explanation should be inferred from the wording alone.

passages.text: After hearing this, I said, “These things can be done, but I do not think that the ability to benefit enemies while enduring every outrage from them can belong to human nature.” Peter answered, “You have spoken correctly. For humaneness, since it is a cause of immortality, is given at great cost.” And I said, “How, then, can it be received into the mind?” Peter answered, “This, my friend Clement, can be acquired if someone becomes fully convinced that enemies who for a time maltreat those they hate become for those people the cause of release from eternal punishment; moreover, those people will love them intensely as benefactors. The path to acquiring this, my friend Clement, is one particular path: the fear of God. For at first the person who fears God cannot love his neighbor as himself, since such a thing does not enter the soul by command. Yet through fear directed toward God he can do what those who love do. Then, once he has thus performed the deeds of love, loving itself, like a bride, is presented to fear as to a bridegroom. And so, as she gives birth to humane thoughts, she makes the one who has acquired her immortal, as an image resembling God, his nature being incapable of violation by decay.” Likewise, after he had set out for us the discourse on humaneness, evening overtook us, and we turned to sleep.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐκ οἴομαι δυνατὸν ἀνθρωπείᾳ προσεῖναι φύσει
lexical_decisions.chosen: I do not think that the ability ... can belong to human nature
lexical_decisions.rationale: προσεῖναι expresses being present in or belonging to something; δυνατός supplies the ability whose presence in human nature Clement doubts.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ φιλανθρωπία πολλοῦ δίδοται
lexical_decisions.chosen: humaneness ... is given at great cost
lexical_decisions.rationale: πολλοῦ δίδοται presents humaneness as something obtained for much or at a high price, not as something easily granted.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Πῶς οὖν σύνεστιν ἐν νῷ λαβεῖν;
lexical_decisions.chosen: How, then, can it be received into the mind?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves both acquisition language in λαβεῖν and the explicitly mental location ἐν νῷ. The question may more idiomatically mean, “How, then, can one acquire it?”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αἰωνίου κολάσεως ἀπαλλαγῆς αὐτοῖς αἴτιοι γίνονται· προσέτι δὲ αὐτοὺς ὡς εὐεργέτας σφόδρα ἀγαπήσουσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: become for those people the cause of release from eternal punishment; moreover, those people will love them intensely as benefactors
lexical_decisions.rationale: The sufferers are taken as the referents of αὐτοῖς and as the understood subject of ἀγαπήσουσιν, while αὐτούς refers back to the enemies. Repeating “those people” makes the selected referents clear without changing the claim.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπεὶ τὸ τοιοῦτο κελεύσει οὐ προσέρχεται τῇ ψυχῇ
lexical_decisions.chosen: since such a thing does not enter the soul by command
lexical_decisions.rationale: κελεύσει is taken instrumentally: love does not arise in the soul merely through being commanded.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ ἀγαπᾶν ὡς νύμφη οὖσα προσφέρεται ὡς νυμφίῳ τῷ φόβῳ
lexical_decisions.chosen: loving itself, like a bride, is presented to fear as to a bridegroom
lexical_decisions.rationale: The personification and bridal image are preserved. τὸ ἀγαπᾶν is formally an infinitive, so “loving itself” retains the emphasis on the act or condition of loving.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοὺς φιλανθρώπους τίκτουσα λογισμοὺς
lexical_decisions.chosen: as she gives birth to humane thoughts
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine pronoun follows the immediately preceding bride imagery, and τίκτουσα retains the explicit image of giving birth.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς εἰκόνα θεοῦ ὁμοίαν, ὑπὸ φθορᾶς ὑβρισθῆναι μὴ δυναμένην τὴν αὐτοῦ φύσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: as an image resembling God, his nature being incapable of violation by decay
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὁμοίαν is taken with the image as resembling God. ὑβρίζω is rendered “violation” to preserve its stronger force than simple damage, while φθορά is “decay” or “corruption.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁμῶς τὸν τῆς φιλανθρωπίας ἐκθεμένου ἡμῖν λόγον
lexical_decisions.chosen: Likewise, after he had set out for us the discourse on humaneness
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐκθεμένου is a genitive singular aorist middle participle of ἐκτίθημι, here carrying the transitive sense “having set out.” Peter is supplied contextually as its understood subject, and λόγον is its accusative object. The printed ὁμῶς is rendered “likewise”; “together” or “equally” remains possible.

source_issues.source_quote: ὁμῶς τὸν τῆς φιλανθρωπίας ἐκθεμένου ἡμῖν λόγον
source_issues.issue: The genitive singular aorist middle participle ἐκθεμένου, here meaning “having set out,” has no explicitly stated genitive subject; Peter is readily supplied from the preceding speech, and λόγον functions as its accusative object. The printed adverb ὁμῶς may mean “likewise,” “equally,” or “together,” whereas the concessive sense “all the same” would normally be written ὅμως. The supplied reading remains defensibly translatable without emendation.
